C01.why: Controls are excellent for touch (thumbstick plus one contextual button, tap-grid CCTV, 4-icon category picker), the scene is light, and 3+5 minute day/night cycles fit a session. However, the core skill is spotting subtle visual changes such as a turning painting or a repeated room number, which is much harder on a 6-inch phone, and a 5-night chapter runs about 40 minutes.
C01.fix: Save progress after every night, so one night equals one session. Make anomalies large silhouette or colour changes rather than fine detail. Add a tap-to-zoom inspect view on CCTV feeds.

C02.why: It is a screen-space puzzle with tap and drag inputs, an emote wheel and 90-second rounds. It needs no avatar movement, has almost no performance cost and is session-perfect. The risks are that dragging the laser puts the finger over the very module being pointed at, and that the grey silhouettes Hands sees may be hard to tell apart on a small screen.
C02.fix: Offset the laser cursor above the touch point and snap it to the nearest module. Set a minimum on-screen size for each module (about 15% of screen height on phone), and use shape plus pattern rather than shades of grey.

C03.why: One hold button and an auto-follow camera are about as mobile-native as 3D gets, and 3–4 minute courses fit any session. The main risk is technical: a single physics raft driven by up to 6 players' inputs over mobile networks may feel laggy or rubber-band, and water physics can strain low-end devices.
C03.fix: Use scripted buoyancy instead of fluid physics. Run the raft with server-authoritative movement plus client-side visual prediction of each player's own thruster. Put the hold button in the jump-button zone and the LEFT/RIGHT/STOP pings in a top-right strip.

C04.why: Tapping and dragging tools over items is natural on touch (Papers, Please works on phones), the NPC load is low and the camera is static. But inspecting small tells such as stamps and paint against a reference catalogue is detail work that a 6-inch screen struggles with, and no shop-day length is given.
C04.fix: Add a full-screen inspection mode with pinch-zoom, and a side-by-side catalogue card that auto-opens for the item type. Define a 5–7 minute shop day with a save at day end.

C05.why: The 6-minute round fits a session, but the game rests on precise physics grab, throw and hide in cluttered indoor rooms. Touch grabbing is imprecise, interior cameras clip, and hundreds of unanchored cups, paint and debris across 7 players will hurt weak Android devices.
C05.fix: Use auto-grab-nearest, plus snap 'Hide here' hotspots (under rug, behind sofa) that trigger from one contextual button. Cap unanchored parts per room, render cosmetic debris client-side, and use a fixed over-shoulder interior camera.

C06.why: Tapping and grid drag-placing are standard tycoon touch inputs, and incremental play suits drop-in mobile sessions. Every plot's conveyors, sifters and a shrinking shared haystack are rendered server-wide, which is a known low-end performance drain, and there is no natural session end or round.
C06.fix: Stream out or LOD other players' plots, and simulate hay flow as numbers with visual particles only near the player. Add a 5-minute 'shift' goal with a payout screen to give sessions an end point.

C07.why: Snap-to-ledge helps, but vertical climbing needs camera control, timed jumps and a reactive Anchor button all at once, which is the hardest combination on touch. Rope constraints between characters over mobile latency produce jitter, and a daily mountain will likely run well past 10 minutes.
C07.fix: Add an auto-framing vertical camera that keeps the whole team in shot, and an auto-anchor when a teammate falls within a short grace window. Split each mountain into 6–8 minute stages that save at each campsite.

C08.why: Three inputs and 6-minute expeditions fit mobile well, and the scoring montage is passive viewing. But framing ghosts with the camera needs a second thumb to steer the view while moving, and dark horror scenes are hard to read on phone screens outdoors or at low brightness.
C08.fix: Add generous auto-framing and soft aim assist toward the nearest ghost event while recording, plus an on-screen 'IN FRAME' meter. Add a brightness or gamma slider and give ghosts strong rim-light so they stay readable.

C09.why: Finger-drawn runes are a genuinely touch-first mechanic that is worse on mouse. But in landscape the drawing is done with the right thumb, which hides the action, takes the hand off camera control, and is imprecise when 'accuracy and speed set power'. Ten-minute waves with many monsters plus combo effects also load low-end devices.
C09.fix: Limit the alphabet to about 6 bold, forgiving shapes, score power on completion rather than accuracy, and auto-target the nearest lane so no camera input is needed. Cap active enemies and particle counts on mobile quality levels.

C10.why: Tap-and-drag on a small board with auto-battles, no avatar movement or camera input, very light rendering and 10-minute runs make it a natural fit for a phone session. The risk is information density: traits, mutations and the family tree can turn into unreadable text on a 6-inch screen.
C10.fix: Show traits and mutations as large icons with tap-and-hold tooltips instead of text lists. Make the family tree a swipeable card stack rather than a sprawling graph.

C11.why: The thumbstick, Grab and Crouch layout is fine, but noise-based stealth in dark rooms is harder to read and control on touch, where thumbstick pressure gives poor speed control. The run length is unspecified, and extraction formats tend to run past 10 minutes.
C11.fix: Show a large on-screen noise ring, and make crouch a toggle that also caps speed. Set contracts at 6–8 minutes with a forced extraction timer.

C12.why: Role panels (engineer taps, navigator map pings) are native touch UIs, and the camera demands are low. Tilt steering is unreliable and uncomfortable on phones, three role UIs triple the readability work, and flight length is not specified.
C12.fix: Replace tilt with a large virtual drag yoke, put incoming pings in a fixed top banner the pilot can read without looking away, and target 4–6 minute flights.

C13.why: Fifty players on one map at 6-inch scale leaves territory, troop counts and borders tiny. Constant map updates for 50 players are expensive in Roblox GUI or parts, and 15-minute rounds where backgrounding the app means losing are a poor fit for mobile sessions.
C13.fix: Cut to 16–20 players on province-based regions (large tap targets, no per-pixel territory) with pinch-zoom, run 8-minute rounds, and let AI take over a disconnected player's territory for 60 seconds.

C14.why: Fragile physics carrying punishes exactly the imprecision that touch and mobile latency create, two-person carries over the network are jittery, and driving needs on-screen pedals plus steering. A physics van, parcels and street hazards are heavy on low-end devices, and no shift length is given.
C14.fix: Use magnetic or assisted carry with damage thresholds tuned for touch, and auto-throttle driving where the player only steers. Set 5-minute shifts with 2–3 deliveries each.

C15.why: Drag-and-drop on a 4x4 board is adapted from an actual mobile hit (Merge Tactics). It needs no thumbstick or camera input, has very light rendering and a fixed 8-minute match, which makes it the most phone-native concept here. The one risk is the 30-second shared-conveyor draft, which can become a latency and tap-speed race that disadvantages weaker connections.
C15.fix: Turn the conveyor into simultaneous picks, where each player picks privately from a shared offer and ties are resolved server-side by turn order, and use large toy cards for picking.

C16.why: No controls or job length are written. Overcooked-style timed chores plus chasing escaped pets imply precise movement and grabbing on touch, though the scenes are light and cozy pacing can forgive imprecision.
C16.fix: Specify thumbstick plus one contextual action button with auto-grab-nearest, and 4–6 minute jobs with a rating screen at the end.

C17.why: Turn-based tap-to-rotate and drag-to-place is touch-friendly and session-friendly. But the dragging finger covers the drop point, depth placement is ambiguous if the scene is 3D, and replicated stacking physics can jitter or desync between clients.
C17.fix: Lock play to a 2D side-view plane, show a ghost preview offset above the finger, and simulate the tower on the server with a single authoritative stack.

C18.why: No controls are specified. Gather, vote and train suits short drop-in sessions, but the payoff is a fixed weekly Saturday battle many mobile players will miss, and crowds around a giant monster in a persistent server are a moderate performance cost.
C18.fix: Make the weekly battle an asynchronous replay viewable any time, with a short tap-to-cheer interaction, and define daily 5-minute care tasks with one-button controls.

C19.why: Three buttons is reasonable, but freezing on time needs fast release-and-press under mobile latency, which can feel unfair. The Guard has to aim a flashlight while scanning about 30 statues for subtle movement on a small screen, and no round length is given.
C19.fix: Auto-freeze statues when the thumbstick is released, and give a short latency-grace window. Tie the Guard's flashlight to camera direction with a wide cone and a highlight on recently moved statues, and set 5-minute rounds.

C20.why: 'Tap where you want the ball to go' is a promising touch-first input, and matches to 11 fit a session. But the pitch doesn't say whether players also move with the thumbstick, and a real-time timing sport over mobile networks needs careful lag handling.
C20.fix: Specify auto-positioning so the tap is the only input, add a generous timing window with server-side lag compensation, and keep the HUD to score plus one ping strip.

overall_notes: The strongest mobile fits avoid continuous 3D avatar precision. Screen-space or board games (C15, C02, C10) and one-button control (C03) top the list. Physics-carry, climbing and chaos concepts (C05, C07, C14) and the 50-player map (C13) are the weakest on touch precision, low-end performance and session length. A recurring gap across pitches is unspecified round or job length (C04, C11, C12, C14, C16, C19) and missing control specs (C16, C18). Horror and anomaly concepts need explicit readability work for small, dark screens. Every concept should state where its HUD sits relative to the default thumbstick and jump zones.
